criteria: Calling `flattenTokens(tokens)` leaves the passed-in tokens object deeply unchanged (the input still deep-equals its pre-call value after the call).

The tokens returned by `flattenTokens` share no nested object or array with the input: mutating a returned token's nested sub-properties (an object-valued `value`, `attributes`, `original`, `path`) leaves the corresponding input token unchanged, and mutating the input afterwards does not alter the previously returned tokens.
`convertTokenData` leaves its input deeply unchanged for every supported input→output combination (object/map/array → object/map/array), including the same-type conversions.

No two tokens produced by a single `convertTokenData` result alias each other or alias the input collection: mutating a token's nested sub-properties in the output does not affect the input collection or any sibling token in the same output.

Existing conversion results are preserved: all current object/map/array round-trips still produce deeply equal results as before, the prototype-pollution protection for malicious `key` values still holds, and both DTCG (`$value`) and non-DTCG (`value`) token syntax keep working.
description:
The public token-handling utilities `flattenTokens` and `convertTokenData` are documented/used as pure, non-mutating helpers, but they only make shallow copies of the token objects they emit. `flattenTokens` builds each result token with `{ ...slice[key], key }`, which copies only the token's top-level properties; nested structures such as an object-valued `value` (composite/DTCG tokens), `attributes`, `original`, and `path` remain shared with the input. `convertTokenData` has the same defect on every conversion path: map→array spreads the token shallowly (`{ key, ...value }`), while array→map and map/array→object reuse the exact token object references from the input. As a result, callers can accidentally mutate their input dictionary by writing to a sub-property of a returned token (e.g. `result[0].attributes.foo = 'bar'` or editing a property of an object value), and mutations to the input after a call retroactively change previously returned results.

Expected behavior: these utilities should be pure. Calling them must not modify the input, and the structures they return must not alias any nested object/array belonging to the input, so that mutating a returned token's sub-properties cannot leak back into the input (and vice versa). The fix should use a full/deep clone rather than a shallow clone, consistent with how the rest of the codebase already clones tokens (`structuredClone` is used in `tokenSetup`, `transformToken`, `resolveObject`, `stripMeta`, `expandObjectTokens`).

Root cause: shallow spread / direct reference reuse when producing flattened token arrays and converted token collections, instead of a deep clone of each token.

none

## BLOCKING
none

## ADVISORY
1. **LOW — sibling aliasing survives in one branch.** `lib/utils/convertTokenData.js:130` (`object → object`) does a single `structuredClone(tokens)` of the whole tree, so if the input tokens share a nested sub-object (e.g. a JS token file reusing one `value`/`attributes` literal across two tokens), the *result* tokens still share it and mutating one changes a sibling. Every other branch clones per token (`lib/utils/flattenTokens.js:27`, `lib/utils/convertTokenData.js:88,101,108,118,126`), so the "returned tokens never alias each other" property is uniform everywhere except here. No in-repo caller reaches it (`StyleDictionary.js:350` and `:597` both pass map/array input), so this is cosmetic today; per-token cloning on a tree walk would make the guarantee unconditional.

2. **LOW — dictionary view identity change (as the account notes).** `lib/StyleDictionary.js:595-598` now returns three views built from separate clones, and `lib/filterTokens.js:87-89` builds `tokenMap` from clones while `allTokens`/`tokens` keep the originals — so within one filtered dictionary the three views disagree in identity. I checked every in-repo consumer: `lib/transform/token.js:78` already clones (`structuredClone(token)`), `lib/utils/references/getReferences.js:66` pushes `{...ref}` copies, `lib/utils/references/outputReferencesFilter.js:31` matches by `token.name`, `getReferences`/`outputReferencesTransformed` look refs up by path. Nothing in-repo depends on identity, so no regression here — but an external format/plugin that mutates a token taken from `dictionary.tokenMap` and reads it via `dictionary.tokens` (or vice versa) will now silently see stale data.

3. **LOW — extra full deep copies of the token set.** The pipeline now clones the whole dictionary roughly twice at init (`StyleDictionary.js:340-341`), twice per platform export (`:595-597`), and once per filtered file (`lib/filterTokens.js:88`), on top of the three pre-existing `structuredClone`s at `StyleDictionary.js:429-433` and the per-token one in `transformToken`. All linear and bounded (no unbounded growth, no I/O), so not a smell-list hit — just constant-factor cost that would be worth a clone-once/convert-many shape if large dictionaries × many output files ever show up in profiles.

4. **LOW — `structuredClone` value semantics on exotic token values.** It throws `DataCloneError` on function-valued token props and silently drops symbol-keyed/non-enumerable props and flattens class instances to plain objects (`DesignToken.value` is typed `any`, so such values are legal). This is not a new constraint the change introduces — `_exportPlatform` (`lib/StyleDictionary.js:429-433`) and `transformToken` (`lib/transform/token.js:78`) already `structuredClone` whole tokens — so the same inputs already failed or degraded before this round. The one genuinely new behavior is `object → object` (`lib/utils/convertTokenData.js:130`), which previously returned the input untouched (preserving those props) and now drops them.

notes:
Scope is limited to the two utilities named in the issue — `flattenTokens` and `convertTokenData`. Other token utilities mentioned as "probably others" are out of scope for this ticket; if the same aliasing defect is found elsewhere, track it separately rather than expanding this change.

Gotchas to respect:
- `structuredClone` cannot clone non-cloneable values (functions, symbols, class instances). Token files loaded from JavaScript can contain such values; the codebase already guards against this in `lib/utils/loadFile.js` (try/catch around `structuredClone`). Whatever deep-clone approach is used must not make these utilities throw where they previously worked.
- These are public, documented APIs (`style-dictionary/utils`). Do not change their call signatures or exported names; `flattenTokens` is marked `@deprecated` in `lib/utils/index.js` but must keep behaving correctly.
- Deep cloning is more expensive than a shallow spread; avoid cloning the same token repeatedly within a single call where it is not needed, but do not sacrifice the non-aliasing guarantee.
- Existing tests in `__tests__/utils/flattenTokens.test.js` pass an array/object as the second argument ("should return the same array" and the DTCG case), which does not match the current `(tokens, usesDtcg)` signature; do not treat those as authoritative behavior to preserve.
- Non-mutation is already the established expectation for sibling utilities (see the 'should not mutate the input' tests for `stripMeta` and `resolveObject`), so new tests should follow that pattern.
